The width of each confidence interval increases over time because uncertainty generally grows as the forecast horizon extends. For the 1-day interval, the range of [199.5, 204.8] reflects low uncertainty, given the limited window for variability or external disruptions. At a one-month horizon, the interval broadens significantly to [190.0, 221.0], capturing the full range of possible scenarios as more unknowns and compounding factors, like economic developments or system shocks, contribute to greater variability.

Specific risks or events could push outcomes outside these intervals, though the probabilities of such occurrences are, by design, relatively small for a 90% confidence interval. In the short term, unexpected announcements or data releases, such as earnings reports or geopolitical developments, could cause sharp deviations. Over longer horizons, larger uncertainties come into play, such as systemic economic changes, policy shifts, or major market disruptions. For instance, in the 1-month horizon, an unforeseen economic crisis or major breakthrough could move the variable well beyond the predicted range. My intervals aim to cover most outcomes, but no forecast can fully account for every extreme or black-swan event.
